title: The nails weighed again at Ceann fhada
summary: The river-fishers and pilots of Ceann fhada, paid by weight in iron nails for the foreshore under the new coal quay, carry their nails to the fish-shed and weigh each man's share again on the old beam they weigh salmon on. Every share is true to the ounce. A pilot enters in the roll of Ceann fhada that the weight was true and the men ashamed.

title: The first coal barge goes down from Ceann fhada
summary: Carts from the pit at Muileann chrom tip the first coal into a flat barge moored against the new quay at Ceann fhada. Two pilots of the hamlet, paid by A' Chompanaidh, take her down the Abhainn uaine at the sweeps, since no one else knows the river.

title: Gormshuil nic Fhearchair reads Wren's grammar to the custodians
summary: At the Samhain sitting of the council at Cathair dhearg, Gormshuil nic Fhearchair reads Samuel Wren's grammar aloud to the custodians of the hills and puts it into Dia-thìris. She tells them that in the humans' tongue a keeper is one who has a thing and holds it until paid. Beathag Dhubh of Doire mhòr enters in her roll that the strangers' book calls the custodians keepers.

title: A hawk-priest's note beside the three words
summary: In the copy of Wren's grammar kept by the hawk-priests of Cnoc bheag, a priest writes in the margin beside the humans' name for the custodians, in Dia-thìris, that Wren writes as a man counts sacks, and signs it with a hawk's head.

title: The custodians of the hills called on the contracts
summary: At the dark of the year the council at Cathair dhearg calls the custodians of the hills to say what their villages make of the contracts coming up from Muileann chrom. It hears four days of talk of iron, lamp-oil and the ton, and makes no ruling.

title: The bell rung once before the fleet was out
summary: On the morning of its hanging the iron bell of the chapel on the quay at Ros dhomhain is rung for the first service while the fishers are loading their boats in silence, as the rule of that quay requires. The crews unload and go home. Three boats of more than twenty go out on the lake that day.

title: The chapel bell kept until the fleet is out
summary: At the chapel door the custodian of Ros dhomhain tells the minister, with Samuel Wren putting it into the humans' tongue, that a bell over the water before the boats are out is the bell for the drowned. The minister agrees at once, and the bell is rung thereafter only when the last boat is clear of the harbour mouth.

title: The contract carried up to Doire mhòr
summary: A boy of Muileann chrom carries a contract of A' Chompanaidh up to Doire mhòr, naming the south slope of its hill under the oaks for a working. Beathag Dhubh has it read to her twice in the mill-house at Muileann chrom by the young man of Ros dhomhain who puts A' Chompanaidh's words into Dia-thìris.

title: Beathag calls Doire mhòr's households to the hearth
summary: On the evening the day for the marks goes by, Beathag Dhubh calls the seven households of Doire mhòr to her fire and has the contract told to them. They talk of iron, oats and sheep. The oldest woman of the hill says that the hill is not theirs, and the households give the answer to the custodian to give.

title: The agent's report sent down from Muileann chrom
summary: The agent of A' Chompanaidh who climbed to Doire mhòr writes that night at the pit-office by the mill that the custodian heard him out in the rain, did not ask him in, and answered that the hill was not hers to sell nor his to buy. He sends it to Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir with the week's figures and advises that the working be opened elsewhere.

title: The road pegged across Doire mhòr's fields and moved
summary: Surveyors of A' Chompanaidh peg the line of the new cart-road from Cnoc fhiadhaich straight across the three best fields of Doire mhòr. Beathag Dhubh sends word to the custodian of Muileann chrom that the fields are in no contract. Five days later the surveyors pull their pegs and lay the line round the foot of the field walls, a mile the longer.

title: Fenn's lens carried to Tobar dhearg
summary: The great glass for the new tower on the southern cape, ground over the sea, is carried from Ros dhomhain to Tobar dhearg on a cart packed in straw. James Fenn sets it in the lamp-room of the tower Torcall Clachair has raised over the old fire-tower.

title: The cart-road round Doire mhòr finished
summary: Hill men paid in iron finish the cart-road of A' Chompanaidh from Cnoc fhiadhaich round the fields of Doire mhòr to the quay at Ceann fhada, with a timber bridge at the lower ford of the Doire mhòr stream. The first loaded carts come round the bend in the autumn.

title: The carters water their horses at Doire mhòr
summary: The carters on the new road ask Beathag Dhubh's leave to water their horses at the stream where the road crosses it below Doire mhòr, and she gives it. In wet weather they eat their bread under the oaks before the last pull down to the river.

title: Anna nic Dhòmhnaill's tally of lit nights cut on the stair wall
summary: Anna nic Dhòmhnaill, keeper of Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg, who cannot write, begins her count on the wall of the tower stair below the lamp-room: one stroke cut with a knife for every night the light is lit, and a stroke across every thirty.

title: The answer of the coast read in the hills
summary: The council at Cathair dhearg copies the answer of the custodians of the north-western coast to Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir over the stripped brig, that those waters have always kept their own law, and sends it round the districts. It is read out at the mill at Muileann chrom.

title: Beathag writes the road into the roll of Doire mhòr
summary: Under the sixteenth year Beathag Dhubh enters in the roll of Doire mhòr the answer of the coast word for word, and then the road round the village's fields, a mile the longer and well built, with two words after it: for now.
